$comment: The six roles of the table in Overview §5, one row each (does, duty = trust duty, economics = economic participation); check-data.mjs fails when the count differs. scenarios are four stories in which the roles work together, each step resting on Overview §5, Connector setup §5 or the recovery table of CLPR Service §7 (rows R2 and R4, named in recovery). The Stories simulation lights a role when a step names it, so steps name roles as the table does.

roles.name: Application developer
roles.does: Deploys the application on both ledgers, chooses the channels and connectors it uses, and handles replies.
roles.economics: Pays connectors, on each connector's own terms.

roles.name: Connector operator
roles.does: Registers and funds a connector on both ledgers of a channel, and often opens the channel.
roles.duty: Vets the verifier contract before staking on the channel.
roles.economics: Funds execution and posts a stake that can be slashed.

roles.name: Verifier developer
roles.does: Publishes verifier contracts for a proof scheme. Has no identity on any ledger.

roles.name: Endpoint operator
roles.does: Runs CLPR Endpoints, which sync with peers and submit bundles. On Hiero every consensus node is an endpoint; on EVM ledgers endpoints register and are admitted by the administrator.
roles.duty: Serves every channel of its ledger.
roles.economics: Pays transaction fees and earns the margin on executed messages. Endpoints are not slashed.

roles.name: CLPR Service administrator
roles.does: Configures the CLPR Service, admits endpoints where admission is curated, and closes channels. Cannot open channels or register connectors.
roles.duty: Acts when a channel is compromised.

scenarios.name: Opening a new route
steps: A verifier developer publishes a verifier contract.
A connector operator vets it, opens the channel, and registers a connector on both ledgers.
An application developer vets the channel and the connector, and uses them.
End users vet the application and use it.

scenarios.name: Proof format change
steps: The peer ledger changes its proof format, and the channel's verifier can no longer check its bundles.
A verifier developer publishes a verifier contract for the new format.
A connector operator registers a new channel with it and registers a connector on both ledgers.
Application developers migrate to the new channel.
The CLPR Service administrator closes the old channel.

scenarios.name: Responding to a compromised verifier
steps: A channel's verifier is found to be compromised or broken.
The CLPR Service administrator closes the channel. While it closes, it still processes incoming bundles, so closing alone does not stop the verifier from being used.
A verifier developer publishes a correct verifier contract, and a connector operator registers a new channel with it.
Application developers vet the new channel and move to it.
Messages in flight on the old channel can be left without a reply; applications reconcile them outside the protocol.

scenarios.name: Withdrawing a connector
steps: The connector operator stops authorizing new messages, so new sends through the connector are rejected.
Messages already in flight are delivered and answered as usual.
Once every message in flight has its reply, the operator removes the connector on both ledgers; removal is refused while any message is in flight.
In the recommended design, the CLPR Service returns the remaining stake to a recipient the connector's admin names.
